hints: Split the term into its two words and link each word to what you can see in Fig. 6.1 - one word describes how the main layer behaves, the other describes how the large structures are arranged in it.
Think about which molecules are able to move sideways past each other, and how the different proteins are spread out like separate pieces within the phospholipid bilayer.
walkthrough:
What Fluid Really Means**
Think of the bilayer not as a solid wall but as a crowded layer of phospholipids that can slide past each other sideways and rotate. That constant lateral movement makes the membrane flexible and lets proteins drift within it.

What Mosaic Really Means**
Now look at the large shapes stuck through the bilayer in Fig. 6.1. They are different types of proteins dotted about at intervals, like tiles in a mosaic. So mosaic means many individual proteins scattered through the continuous phospholipid bilayer.
Final answer: fluid - phospholipids (and proteins) can move laterally; mosaic - proteins / glycoproteins are scattered / embedded in different positions in the phospholipid bilayer.

hints: Recall the scale at which membranes are seen - they are far too thin for a light microscope and are measured in nanometres, only a few molecules thick.
walkthrough:
Remembering the True Scale**
A cell surface membrane is only two phospholipids thick plus proteins, so it is extremely thin. You need a transmission electron microscope to see it, and its thickness is about $7 \text{ nm}$.

hints: Start by listing what you can already see in Fig. 6.1 - a phospholipid bilayer with some intrinsic proteins - then ask what normal membrane molecules are missing from the drawing.
Think about the small molecule that sits between the fatty acid tails in animal cell membranes and controls fluidity.
Think about the sugary coating on the outside of the cell - what happens when short carbohydrate chains are attached to proteins or to lipids?
Think about the variety of proteins - not just the general blobs shown, but specific transport proteins and proteins that sit on the surface or act as signals.
walkthrough:
Spot What Is Missing Between the Tails**
Fig. 6.1 shows heads and tails and a few big proteins, but it leaves out cholesterol. In eukaryotic membranes cholesterol lies tucked between the phospholipid fatty acid tails and helps regulate fluidity and stability.

Add the Sugar Coating on the Outside**
A real cell surface has short branched carbohydrate chains sticking out into the exterior. When attached to protein they form glycoproteins, when attached to lipid they form glycolipids. Together they form the glycocalyx used for recognition and adhesion.

Name the Specialist Proteins**
The diagram shows only generic intrinsic proteins. In reality there are channel proteins including aquaporins for facilitated diffusion, carrier proteins for active transport and facilitated diffusion, and peripheral / extrinsic proteins sitting on the inner or outer surface.

Include Signalling and Support Links**
Two other real features are receptor proteins for hormones and other signals, and cell surface antigens for recognition. On the inside, many proteins are anchored to the cytoskeleton / microfilaments for support. Any four of these valid missing features gain full credit.

Final answer: Any four from: cholesterol between phospholipids; glycoproteins (carbohydrate chains on proteins); glycolipids (carbohydrate chains on lipids) / glycocalyx; channel proteins e.g. aquaporin; carrier proteins; peripheral / extrinsic proteins; receptor proteins; antigen / cell recognition proteins; attachment to cytoskeleton.
